name: PPA (Polyphthalamide / High-Temp Nylon)
chemical_makeup: Semi-aromatic polyamide in which part of the aliphatic diacid is replaced by a phthalic-acid-derived aromatic unit. The rigid aromatic ring in the backbone raises Tg from PA6's ~60 °C to ~125 °C and the melting point to ~305 °C, and simultaneously cuts moisture uptake — the whole property set follows from that one substitution. Commercial FDM PPA is almost always compounded with chopped carbon fiber (PPA-CF) or glass fiber (PPA-GF15/GF30).
summary: The high-temperature tier of the polyamide family and the hardest material in this catalog outside the PEEK class. Deltas vs the base pa entry: melting point ~305 °C against PA6's ~220 °C, Tg 125 °C against ~50 °C, HDT from 196 °C @1.8 MPa (Bambu PPA-CF) to 260 °C (3DXTech PPA-GF15), tensile up to 168 MPa X-Y, and saturated water absorption of only ~1.3 %. It pays for all of it with the family's most extreme process window: 280-390 °C nozzle, 100-160 °C bed, a heated chamber, a hardened nozzle and 100-140 °C drying — plus roughly triple the price of pa6.

printing.notes: Two very different hardware tiers hide inside this window and the recommended values follow the prosumer one. Bambu's PPA-CF runs 280-310 °C nozzle (0.6 mm recommended), 100-120 °C bed and a 50-80 °C chamber; 3DXTech's FibreX PPA-GF15 runs 365-390 °C nozzle, 140-160 °C bed and a chamber up to 140 °C on what it explicitly calls industrial-grade hardware. heated_chamber_required is recorded true — it is the only grade in this family to earn that, and the flag is what separates PPA from pa6/pa12/pa66, whose enclosures are passive. Chamber heat retention is critical against delamination, so never open the door: enclosure_open_for_cooling is false and part cooling stays at 0 %. requires_hardened_nozzle is true because essentially every commercial PPA filament is CF- or GF-filled, and fibre abrasion at these temperatures wears a nozzle faster than in any PA6/PA12 composite; neat unfilled PPA would not need one but is not realistically available.

feeding.notes: Stiff, brittle, fiber-filled filament needing an all-metal high-temperature hotend and a well-tuned extruder with good grip — direct drive is the sensible default, and long Bowden paths risk snapping the low-elongation strand. No shore hardness and no feeding assistant (not an elastomer). AMS status is 'conditional' in the narrowest sense: Bambu positions PPA-CF alongside the high-temperature AMS HT unit rather than the standard AMS, since standard units are neither rated for the drying/handling regime nor tolerant of fibre wear on their PTFE paths (unverified exact wording). Third-party PPA-CF/GF should be treated as barred from a standard AMS outright. Feed from a heated drybox at <20 % RH regardless of unit.

methods: heated-bed method at 110-120 °C for 12 h (less effective)
sealed drybox with desiccant at <20 % RH while printing
drying.dryness_validation: No popping or steam at the nozzle and no voids or fuzz in a purge line — gloss is a poor indicator because the fiber-filled extrudate is matte by design. At these nozzle temperatures residual moisture shows up as visible foaming almost immediately, so the purge line is a reliable test.
drying.notes: The highest drying requirement in the catalog outside the PEEK class and the clearest quantitative separator in the PA family: Bambu specifies 100-140 °C for 8-12 h for PPA-CF and 3DXTech 120 °C for 4 h minimum for PPA-GF15, against pa66's 90 °C, pa6's 80 °C and pa12's 70 °C. PPA's high Tg (125 °C) is what both permits and requires drying this hot — the filament does not soften at temperatures that would slump a PA6 spool, and moisture will not fully desorb below them. Ordinary consumer filament dryers top out around 70-90 °C and are therefore not sufficient for this grade.

storage.recommendations: Sealed with fresh desiccant below 20 % RH at all times, per Bambu's own guidance for PPA-CF, and fed from a heated drybox. PPA absorbs far less water than pa6 or pa66 in absolute terms (~1.3 % saturated), but the consequence of a wet spool is worse: at 300+ °C the trapped water flashes instantly and foams a fiber-filled melt that has little strength to spare.

price.notes: The most expensive grade in the polyamide family by a wide margin — roughly 2-3x filled PA6 and 3-5x unfilled pa6. Bambu PPA-CF is $149.99/750 g (~$200/kg); 3DXTech FibreX PPA-GF15 is ~EUR 140/750 g (~$200/kg), falling to ~EUR 126-168/kg at 10+ units. Both figures are for fiber-filled grades because neat PPA filament is essentially not sold at retail.

recommended: jigs and fixtures for continuous high-temperature service
metal-replacement parts where pa66 lacks the heat capability
not_recommended: any printer without a heated chamber and a 300 °C+ all-metal hotend
consumer filament dryers that cannot reach 100 °C
budget or hobby projects — 3-5x the cost of pa6
parts needing high elongation or impact toughness (Z tensile is ~1/3 of X-Y)
large flat parts printed in a passive enclosure

properties.notes: Density 1.18 g/cm³ is the neat semi-aromatic resin figure; the fiber-filled grades actually sold run heavier — Bambu's PPA-CF measures 1.25 g/cm³, the densest polyamide in this catalog — so budget part weight from 1.25 if buying a CF grade. Tg 125 °C (3DXTech FibreX PPA-GF15) against pa6's 60 °C and pa12's 40 °C is the headline number, and melting point ~305 °C against PA6's ~220 °C explains the process window. HDT is recorded at 260 °C @0.45 MPa from the GF15 datasheet; Bambu's PPA-CF reports 196 °C at the harsher 1.8 MPa load, against 164 °C for PA6-CF and 137 °C for PA12-CF at the same load — every comparison points the same way. Tensile X-Y 168 ± 4 MPa (Bambu PPA-CF) is roughly 1.6x PA6-CF's 102 MPa, but Z tensile is only 57 ± 5 MPa, about a third of X-Y — orient loads in plane. Saturated water absorption 1.30 % (Bambu). Max service temp and shrinkage are reasoned from Tg, HDT and the fiber loading rather than taken from a datasheet.

compatibility.notes: Unlike the aliphatic grades, PPA does not usefully cross-bond within the family: pa6, pa12 and pa66 all melt 40-100 °C below PPA's ~305 °C, so an aliphatic nylon placed against PPA either degrades or fails to fuse — this is the compatibility delta that most distinguishes ppa from its siblings, which bond to each other freely. Same-material or ppa-cf breakaway supports are the only practical option. Soluble supports are out entirely: pva degrades above ~200 °C and bvoh not far above, both far below PPA's process temperatures. Build-plate chemistry needs a high-temperature adhesive; ordinary PA glue sticks are not characterised at a 160 °C bed (unverified).

plate_recommendations.notes: Usable at the Bambu PPA-CF end of the range (100-120 °C bed), which is within the normal comfort zone of a textured PEI sheet. It is the wrong surface for the 3DXTech GF15 end: bed 140-160 °C with a chamber to 140 °C exceeds what many PEI sheets and their adhesive backings are rated for sustained use at (unverified exact ratings, flagged as a likely failure point). Garolite / G10 or another high-temperature composite build surface is the recommendation for those grades — no such plate entry exists in the catalog yet, so it is recorded here in notes.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): High-performance polyamide; bed temps push the lamination adhesive and adhesion is unreliable.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Outside the characterised range for the satin coat.
Backfilled from plate entry (Phase E reciprocity): Far outside the rated range.

alternatives.reason: The filled grade is the one most people can actually print: warp 3 vs 8, ease 3 vs 1 and a cooler 280-315 °C nozzle against PPA's 280-390 °C, with higher strength (compression 10 vs 9) — at $172-266/kg, worse anisotropy (adhesion 3 vs 6) and the catalog's harshest drying schedule.

Roughly half the price ($79-135 vs $150-200) and printable without a true heated chamber, with warp 3 vs 8 — at 40-60 °C less HDT (175-215 vs 196-260 °C, temp 8 vs 9) and PA6's much worse moisture behaviour (water 2 vs 6).

A different route to the same temperature class (temp 9, equal) with far better layer adhesion (8 vs 6), better dimensional stability (8 vs 7) and none of the polyamide hygroscopy — at $195-290/kg and a heated chamber that is equally mandatory.

Same temperature class (temp 9, equal) with far lower warp (3 vs 8), genuine outdoor and chemical resistance (uv 9 vs 3, weather 9 vs 6, water 9 vs 6) and no heated-chamber requirement — often cheaper too ($100-200 vs $150-200), giving up ductility (adhesion 5 vs 6).

The ceiling above PPA (temp 10 vs 9, weather 8 vs 6, water 9 vs 6) when 260 °C HDT is still not enough — at $400-900/kg, equally unprintable without industrial hardware (ease 1, equal) and the catalog's worst warp (10 vs 8).

emissions.notes: Scored the worst in the polyamide family on both axes, and the only one at 'required'. Two compounding reasons: PPA processes at 280-390 °C — 60-120 °C above pa6 — and nylon VOC and ultrafine-particle emission rises steeply with nozzle temperature; and the mandatory heated chamber concentrates whatever is produced inside a sealed volume that is then vented into the room. Active extraction or HEPA+carbon filtration on the enclosure is not optional here. Post-processing filled PPA liberates respirable carbon or glass fibre dust — wet-sand with respiratory protection. No PPA-specific emissions study was found; this is inference from the general nylon temperature relationship plus the chamber requirement (unverified).

safety_notes: Requires an all-metal hotend rated for 300 °C+ (390 °C for the GF15 grades) — a PTFE-lined hotend will decompose its liner and release fluoropolymer breakdown products well below these temperatures. Bed and chamber surfaces reach 140-160 °C and will burn on contact; let the machine cool before reaching in. Drying ovens run at 100-140 °C, hot enough to soften or deform standard plastic spools — check the spool material before oven-drying. Filled grades produce respirable fibre dust when sanded, drilled or machined. Not food-contact suitable.
additional_notes: PPA is where the polyamide family stops being a hobby material. The decision rule against its siblings is simply the service temperature: below ~90 °C use pa6 or pa12, up to ~135 °C use pa66, and only above that does PPA's cost and hardware burden pay for itself. Note also that this entry describes a grade that is sold almost exclusively fiber-filled — the separate ppa-cf entry covers the carbon-filled specifics, and most of the numbers cited here necessarily come from filled datasheets because neat PPA filament is not a retail product. Siraya Tech's four-way comparison rates PPA 'excellent' on mechanical strength and 'high' on thermal stability while rating its printability 'challenging' — the worst of PPA, PA6, PA12 and PA612.

provenance.conflicts: The nozzle window is the largest unresolved disagreement in this catalog: Bambu PPA-CF 280-310 °C vs 3DXTech FibreX PPA-GF15 365-390 °C, with beds at 100-120 °C vs 140-160 °C and chambers at 50-80 °C vs up to 140 °C. These are almost certainly different matrix chemistries and fiber loadings rather than a measurement dispute, but it is unverified which is 'typical' — the recommended values follow Bambu's prosumer grade and the maxima follow 3DXTech's. heated_chamber_required is recorded true on the strength of 3DXTech's industrial-hardware statement, even though Bambu's PPA-CF is printable in a prosumer passively-heated enclosure; treat the flag as 'true for the grade as a class'. Density 1.18 is the neat-resin figure while the only measured filament value found is 1.25 (Bambu PPA-CF, fiber-filled) — the derived weight/volume figures therefore describe neat PPA, not the spool you will buy. HDT is quoted at two different loads by the two vendors (260 °C @0.45 MPa vs 196 °C @1.8 MPa) and is not directly comparable. Max service temp, shrinkage and Tg-to-service-ceiling reasoning are inferred, not sourced. No UV-exposure data was found for PPA — uv_tolerance 3 is a reasoned aromatic-polyamide estimate (unverified). The Bambu wiki page returned HTTP 402 and was cross-checked via the additive-x TDS PDF and a retail listing instead. Emissions are inferred from the nylon temperature relationship, not measured for PPA.
